value.overview: The Costa Rican Pygmy-Owl (Glaucidium costaricanum) is a very small owl of the Central American highlands. It is mainly associated with humid montane forests, especially oak and evergreen woodland, and is often active during daylight as well as at dawn and dusk. Despite its name, the species is not restricted to Costa Rica; it also occurs locally in western Panama. Its small size, bold hunting behavior, and contrasting false eye-spots make it distinctive.
value.classification: The Costa Rican Pygmy-Owl belongs to the owl family Strigidae and the genus Glaucidium, whose members are commonly called pygmy-owls. It is a distinct Central American mountain species.
value.identification: This small, compact owl has a rounded head without ear-tufts, a short tail, and bright yellow eyes, bill, and feet. The usual plumage is dark brown above with pale spotting and a whitish, dark-streaked underside. Rufous individuals also occur. White-edged black markings on the back of the head resemble eyes and may confuse predators or mobbing birds. It can resemble other mountain pygmy-owls, but its Central American range and highland habitat are useful clues.
value.rangeHabitat: The species is found mainly in Costa Rica and western Panama. In Costa Rica, it occurs in the Cordillera Central and Cordillera de Talamanca, including humid highland forests on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes. It generally occupies elevations from roughly 900 meters upward on the Caribbean side and from about 1,200 meters upward on the Pacific side. Typical habitats include mature montane evergreen forest, oak forest, cloud-forest margins, forest edges, and semi-open areas retaining substantial tree cover.
value.migrationStatus: The Costa Rican Pygmy-Owl is considered a year-round resident in Costa Rica and across its limited range. No regular seasonal migration is known, although local movements may occur in response to food availability or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: Breeding information remains limited. The species nests in natural tree cavities and may use old woodpecker holes or other abandoned cavities. A nest recorded in March contained three eggs, suggesting that breeding can occur during the late dry season in Costa Rica, but the full breeding calendar and average clutch size are not well established. As in related pygmy-owls, the female is likely to remain at the nest while the male supplies food, but detailed parental behavior is poorly documented.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet includes insects and other large arthropods, lizards, small birds, small mammals, and possibly other small vertebrates. It commonly hunts from a low or concealed perch in dense foliage, making a short, rapid dash at prey. The owl may forage during the day and at night, with activity often noticeable in the morning, afternoon, and early evening. If an attack fails, it commonly returns to its perch rather than pursuing prey.
value.behavior: The Costa Rican Pygmy-Owl is an alert, active predator that often perches quietly before suddenly darting at prey. It may be detected by its clear, repeated tooting calls, usually given in pairs or short series. Like other pygmy-owls, it can be active in daylight and may attract the attention of small birds that mob it. Agitated individuals may repeatedly swish their tails. It is usually encountered alone or in pairs.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population size has not been determined, but it is generally considered stable. The species is locally fairly common in parts of Costa Rica and rarer and more patchily distributed in western Panama.
